transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-12-20 14:00 UTC
- Duration: ~58 minutes
- Attendees: Eve Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Laura Chen (CISO - Cascade), Marcus Doyle (Head of Infra), Priya Singh (Security Engineer)

Summary:
Short deep dive on Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) security architecture focused on network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, KMS/Encryption, audit logs and compliance posture. Cascade bank looking for enterprise-grade isolation, customer-managed keys, strict egress controls, and auditability to satisfy SOC2/ISO requirements.

Topics covered:
- Deployment models: Private VPC vs on-prem (air gapped) options
- Network isolation patterns: subnets, security groups, NACLs, dedicated clusters
- Ingress design: ALB/private endpoints, bastion, VPN, zero trust
- Egress controls: NAT gateways, egress-only IGW, proxy, explicit deny rules
- Firewalling: NGFWs, cloud firewall rules, IDS/IPS, logging to SIEM
- Encryption/KMS: CMKs vs Redwood-managed keys, HSM support, key rotation
- Audit trails: audit logs, access logs, SIEM integration, retention for compliance

Transcript:
[00:00] Eve: hey everyone, thanks for joining we're super pumped to dig into the private vpc options for cascade bank, um Samir and I will cover network and encryption pieces and then we can go deep on anything you want.
[00:18] Laura: thanks Eve, time is tight so we want to focus on how you achieve strong network isolation and how ingress and egress are controlled, also need to understand KMS key ownership and audit trails for SOC 2.
[00:34] Samir: absolutely. Quick context, Redwood Private runs a control plane that can be customer-managed in a VPC or we can deploy an on-prem package for air-gapped setups. For VPC our standard pattern is to use dedicated subnets for inference clusters, separate management subnets, and strict security group policies.
[00:55] Marcus: when you say control plane, is that in our VPC or in Redwood's? we need the control plane inside our network for this deployment.
[01:06] Samir: yes, for Private we support both models. For the customer-managed control plane the control plane services run in your VPC and talk to the inference nodes over internal endpoints. Redwood provides terraform modules and a deployment artifact. There's also an on-prem option where the control plane is inside your private dmz with no internet egress.
[01:28] Priya: ok and how do you handle ingress, do you use public load balancers? we need to avoid public exposure.
[01:36] Eve: good q. For a fully private setup we use internal ALBs or private NLBs exposed only to your application subnets or via private endpoints. If customers need a narrow ingress surface we recommend a customer-managed API gateway or a mutual TLS front that terminates at the ALB and then mTLS to the service.
[01:56] Samir: also we can put a bastion or jump box in a management subnet for admin activities and we strongly recommend restricting SSH via session manager or SSM-like mechanisms, not open port 22.
[02:10] Marcus: what about peering between Redwood's infra and ours? some vendors ask for peering which we don't allow.
[02:18] Samir: we don't require peering. For customer-managed control plane there is no vendor VPC peering — everything lives in your account/VPC. For hosted models we use encrypted service endpoints and strict routing but that's not applicable here.
[02:32] Laura: audit logs — we need to ship everything to our SIEM (Splunk) and retain for 7 years, is that possible?
[02:39] Samir: yes we emit structured audit logs for API calls, admin actions, and model inference metadata. Those can be routed to your logging endpoints — S3 buckets in your account, Kinesis/firehose to Splunk, or direct syslog for on-prem SIEMs. Retention is up to you; we can configure default retention and lifecycle.
[02:56] Priya: Does the service plane ever send logs outside our VPC?
[03:02] Samir: no not for Private with customer-managed control plane. All logs remain in your account and you control export. For on-prem air-gapped we provide local log collectors.
[03:13] Marcus: firewalling — we're using a Palo Alto NGFW. will Redwood integrate with that for traffic inspection?
[03:20] Samir: yes, traffic flows are standard TCP/TLS and you can route through your NGFW. We recommend inline IDS/IPS for egress inspection; for metadata we push flow logs and application logs to your SIEM. When needed we can provide sample rules for the NGFW to allow internal health checks, inter-node KV cache traffic, and management plane.
[03:38] Eve: important callout — inference nodes talk to each other for KV cache and parameter server traffic, that is kept on private subnets and restricted security groups. We recommend microsegmentation: control plane, inference, and management each in their own subnet with explicit allow lists.
[03:56] Priya: can we enforce network policy at container level, like Calico?
[04:01] Samir: yes if you deploy on-prem we support CNI plugins like Calico for pod-level policies; in cloud VPC we rely on security groups plus optional service mesh for mTLS.
[04:12] Laura: encryption — we need customer-managed keys in an HSM. does Redwood support BYOK?
[04:19] Samir: yes, for Private we support customer-managed CMKs in AWS KMS and bring-your-own-key with CloudHSM backing for HSM-backed keys. Keys stay in your account; Redwood never holds key material. We also support HSM on-prem integrations if you're doing an air-gapped install.
[04:36] Marcus: key rotation and access control — who can perform decrypt? we need fine-grained policies.
[04:43] Samir: you control the KMS key policies. Redwood services get minimal IAM role permissions that you explicitly provision. We recommend a key policy that allows Redwood encr/decr for runtime only and requires separate IAM principals for admin actions. We also support envelope encryption so data at rest in EBS/stores is encrypted with a data key wrapped by the CMK.
[05:04] Priya: do you support HSM-backed attestation, and can we require customer approval for key usage?
[05:11] Samir: we can wire in an approval workflow for key usage using an external KMS and require an approval step via your KMS governance tools; attestation is supported via CloudHSM and we can produce key usage logs for your auditors.
[05:25] Laura: SOC2 — do you have a SOC2 Type II report and scope that covers the Private offering?
[05:31] Eve: yes we have SOC2 Type II and ISO27001, the artifacts cover our control plane offerings; for full coverage on private in-customer accounts we provide supplemental attestation and customer-responsibility matrix. I'll share the report and the RACI.
[05:48] Marcus: what about SSO/SAML and RBAC? we need SSO across console and API, and role-based access control.
[05:56] Samir: we integrate with SAML 2.0 providers for SSO and support SCIM for provisioning. RBAC is declarative — you can define roles for admin, operator, auditor. We also emit token-level audit trails so you can see which user invoked which model call.
[06:13] Priya: token-level audit for inference calls — does that include prompt/response payloads?
[06:19] Samir: we log metadata by default; sensitive payloads can be redacted unless you opt-in to retain full payloads in your S3. For compliance you can choose to store transcripts and we recommend encrypting them with your CMK.
[06:33] Laura: data residency — we must ensure PII doesn't leave EU. how do you constrain region?
[06:39] Samir: you can pin the region at deployment time — the resources and storage are provisioned in that region only. For cross-region backups we require explicit consent.
[06:48] Marcus: egress controls — can you restrict outbound network calls from inference nodes? we want to allow only a proxy to reach external services.
[06:55] Samir: yes you can enforce egress via NAT gateways with explicit allow lists or via a proxy (Squid/Envoy) that inspects traffic. We also support egress-only IGWs and security group denies. In on-prem air-gapped mode there is no external egress unless you explicitly open it.
[07:14] Priya: do you provide a sample ipset of endpoints the nodes might reach during updates or scaling?
[07:20] Samir: yes we have a published list of IP ranges and endpoints for agent updates, metrics, and optional telemetry when enabled. But again, for the customer-managed control plane these are optional and can be disabled. I'll include the list in the follow up.
[07:33] Eve: for firewall rules you'll typically want to allow management plane ports (ports 443 for control, health check ports ephemeral) and inter-node ports for grpc and KV cache. We provide a hardened baseline with explicit port list.
[07:48] Marcus: patching and image scanning — we need assurance that container images are scanned and patched.
[07:53] Samir: our distro pipeline scans images with Clair/Trivy and we publish SBOMs on request. For Private you can run your own registry and image scanning or opt into Redwood's signed images — we support attested images and image signing.
[08:08] Priya: logging pipeline — can we send audit and access logs to our SIEM, and do you support Kafka/Firehose?
[08:14] Samir: yes S3 or Firehose or direct syslog — we can push to Kafka via a connector. We also support structured JSON logs compatible with Splunk and ELK.
[08:25] Laura: for compliance we'll need to map controls to SOC2 trust services and have evidence. can you provide a controls matrix?
[08:31] Eve: yes that's part of the deliverables. We'll provide the SOC2 control mapping and an architecture diagram showing responsibility boundaries.
[08:40] Marcus: on the network side, do you support namespace isolation at the hypervisor level, like dedicated hosts?
[08:46] Samir: if you need physical isolation we can run on dedicated instances or dedicated GPU hosts in your account; that increases cost but gives you tenancy guarantees. For most banks we do dedicated subnets and strong network controls which is sufficient for SOC2/ISO.
[08:59] Priya: what about egress detection — can Redwood emit alerts when a process attempts an outbound connection not in allowlist?
[09:06] Samir: yes, we have host-level agents that can be configured to report suspicious outbound connections to your SIEM and trigger quarantine policies.
[09:15] Laura: what's the recommended encryption in transit posture?
[09:18] Samir: TLS 1.3 everywhere, mTLS between services for extra assurance, and we support client cert rotation. We recommend enforcing TLS and disabling older ciphers.
[09:29] Marcus: for audits we need key usage logs tied to user identity. can you correlate KMS usage with user actions?
[09:36] Samir: yes KMS logs (CloudTrail/Key Audit) can be correlated with our audit logs — we include request IDs so you can trace a specific decrypt operation back to an API call and user.
[09:48] Priya: are there any default telemetry/phone-home features we should be aware of?
[09:52] Eve: by default telemetry is minimal and disabled in Private; metrics for autoscaling are inside your VPC. Any external telemetry or metrics collection requires opt-in.
[10:01] Laura: excellent. let's talk failure modes — if an inference node is compromised how do we limit blast radius?
[10:08] Samir: microsegmentation and least privilege, container runtime restrictions, ephemeral instances, and EBS encryption. We also support automatic instance replacement and isolating nodes at the subnet level while preserving state in encrypted stores.
[10:24] Marcus: can we have a canary circuit breaker if model outputs deviate or anomalous behavior is detected?
[10:30] Samir: yes we support rollout controls and automatic fallback to a smaller model if anomalies are detected. That ties into our observability and evals and we can trigger alarms to your ops channel.
[10:42] Eve: ok i want to summarize next steps — i'll send SOC2 and ISO artifacts, Samir will share architecture diagram and IP allowlist, Marcus/Priya will send egress requirements and pilot timeline. we'll schedule the on-prem checklist call next week.
[10:58] Laura: sounds good. any outstanding security blockers?
[11:02] Priya: one — we need to validate that key rotation policies fit our infosec policy, but that seems doable.
[11:08] Samir: yep we'll include rotation cadence recommendations and sample KMS policies.
[11:14] Eve: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the docs and action items.
